content: The development of Rhesus immunisation and its prophylactic use since the 1970s has significantly reduced the occurrence of severe Rhesus D (RhD) alloimmunisation. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effects of administering anti-D immunoglobulin to Rhesus-negative women, who do not have pre-existing anti-D antibodies, after giving birth to a Rhesus-positive infant. The search for relevant studies included the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of March 2010) and reference lists of pertinent articles. The review focused on randomised trials involving Rhesus-negative women without anti-D antibodies who were given postpartum anti-D immunoglobulin, compared to those who received no treatment or a placebo. Each author independently assessed the inclusion criteria, trial quality, and extracted data. Initial analyses included all trials, while subsequent analyses examined the impact of trial quality, ABO compatibility, and dosage on outcomes. Six eligible trials, involving over 10,000 women, compared postpartum anti-D prophylaxis with no treatment or placebo. The quality of the trials varied. The administration of anti-D significantly reduced the incidence of RhD alloimmunisation six months after childbirth, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.04 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 0.06). It also reduced the risk of RhD alloimmunisation in subsequent pregnancies, with an RR of 0.12 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.23). These protective effects were observed regardless of the ABO compatibility between the mother and infant, provided that anti-D was administered within 72 hours of delivery. Higher doses of anti-D (up to 200 micrograms) were more effective in preventing RhD alloimmunisation in subsequent pregnancies compared to lower doses (up to 50 micrograms). In conclusion, the administration of anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours after childbirth reduces the risk of RhD alloimmunisation in Rhesus-negative women who have delivered a Rhesus-positive infant. However, the evidence regarding the optimal dose of anti-D remains limited.
